The world

TechCrunch · October 5, 2026

OpenAI opens paid ads inside ChatGPT’s own image generator

OpenAI began rolling out visual display ads that appear next to the images ChatGPT generates, its second ad format after the text-based sponsored links it launched earlier this year. The ads are clearly labeled, OpenAI says they cannot influence what ChatGPT answers or generates, and for now they only appear for people on the Free and the $8-a-month Go tier: anyone paying for Plus, Pro, Business or Enterprise sees none. The US rollout starts this month with an initial group of advertisers, measurement partners including AppsFlyer and Triple Whale, and brand-safety review from DoubleVerify and Integral Ad Science. ChatGPT now reaches 1.2 billion weekly users, the inventory this is built on.

Why it mattersFree version carries ads, paid version doesn’t, the oldest trade in media, now running inside a chatbot. The real news isn’t the ad unit, it’s that OpenAI just drew its own line between the audience it monetizes with attention and the audience it monetizes with a subscription fee.
ppc.land / AdExchanger · October 8, 2026

Apple quietly tests letting The Trade Desk back into Safari

Last issue covered Apple’s new, undisclosed ad-tech blocklist inside Safari on iOS 27. On October 5 at 12:29pm Pacific, Apple engineer John Wilander told The Trade Desk’s Ian Meyers that a new iOS 27.2 beta had shipped removing adsrvr.org, The Trade Desk’s core domain, from the list, and asked him to test it. Fifteen minutes later Meyers confirmed he could see the change, the first two-way conversation Apple has had with anyone on the blocklist about the blocklist. The other eight blocked domains, including identity services uidapi.com and id5-sync.com, are still blocked as of this writing.

Why it mattersThe exchange lasted fifteen minutes and never named a domain, a setting or a reason, per AdExchanger’s reporting. A platform can let one company back in without ever explaining the rule it enforces, leaving the rest of the industry to reverse-engineer its standing from who gets a reply.
Grocery Dive / Digiday · early October 2026

Albertsons folds its retail-media chief’s job into the CMO’s office

Brian Monahan, hired from Dentsu just over a year ago to run Albertsons Media Collective, has left the company; Albertsons says the unit now reports directly to CMO Emily Turner instead of having its own senior vice president. The company has not said whether Monahan’s old role will be filled.

Why it mattersIssue 10 flagged retail media climbing into the CMO’s job description at Target and Lowe’s, as a promotion. At Albertsons it is the opposite move: the dedicated retail-media seat disappears into marketing entirely. Same trend, read two ways, either retail media has arrived so completely it no longer needs its own chair, or it never built enough independent weight to keep one.
Digiday · October 9, 2026

The WNBA’s newest team becomes the first women’s sports team past $100 million

Golden State Valkyries president Jess Smith told Digiday the team, only in its second season, has crossed $100 million in annual revenue with more than 40 sponsors, sponsorship revenue alone up 30% year over year, backed by an 8-person internal team that tracks partnership performance data for brands. Next season adds six more home games, a 15% increase. Smith’s pitch to sponsors: “mission and capital can coexist.”

Why it mattersSmith’s other line, that exclusivity “is important for teams too,” is the detail worth keeping. She is not selling access at a discount because the cause is good, she is pricing it like scarce inventory. That is a different sales conversation than women’s sports marketing usually gets credit for having.

Campaigns & brand moves

Publicis Conseil · October 11, 2026

Orange turns the sound of being scammed into a jingle

Orange and Publicis Conseil built “Scamcophonie,” a spot that strings together the ringtones, vibrations, pop-up alerts and unwanted calls of a day spent fending off phishing attempts into an actual musical composition, before resolving into silence when Orange Cybersecure shuts the noise off. Directors Bradley & Pablo shot it with production company Wanda; agency Razorfish handles the social cut. It runs on French TV and online video from October 11 to November 1.

Why it mattersMost cybersecurity advertising shows the threat, then the shield. This one skips the threat and sells the feeling of the noise finally stopping, a more honest description of what the product actually buys you.
Contentgrip · October 3, 2026

Mastercard turns payment fraud into a Korean drama

“Tap Into My Heart” is a three-episode K-microdrama Mastercard built with McCann Singapore, using the genre’s own conventions, suspicion, misdirection, a slow-build romance, to carry a payment-security message instead of a voiceover explaining one. It rolls out across Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam and the Philippines over eight weeks, full episodes on YouTube and cutdowns on TikTok and Meta. Mastercard’s SVP for Southeast Asia, Dheeraj Raina, said the goal was to stop making “awareness campaigns consumers could easily tune out.”

Why it mattersThe format choice is the strategy. K-dramas already have the region’s attention, Mastercard is renting that attention instead of competing with it for a 30-second slot.
Maybelline New York / NAMI · October 10, 2026

Maybelline spends World Mental Health Day on the people who show up

“Together We’re Brave,” the newest chapter of Maybelline’s Brave Together program, turns its cameras on the friend, the mother, the daughter who sits with someone through anxiety or depression, instead of the person experiencing it. Since 2020 the program has funded free one-to-one mental health support for more than 4 million people, through partnerships with 45 nonprofits across 37 countries and close to $10 million committed globally.

Why it mattersMost mental health marketing centers the sufferer and asks the audience to feel for them. This one centers the supporter and asks the audience to recognize themselves, a small reframe that changes who the ad is actually talking to.

What is working in content

Digiday · October 9, 2026

Top creators are taking fewer brand deals, not more

Alix Earle, 14 million followers, told Digiday she would rather work with “five or six brands than 100 every year.” Jordan Howlett became Chief Content Officer at Blenders Eyewear, shaping product design (the brand now sells “Jordan-proof” reinforced hinges) and directing its commercials. Kevin Cooney, 4 million followers, turns down most inbound and runs his own brand integrations through a repeatable “Mad Libs” formula built on formats he already knows work. Issa Rae’s HOORAE Media gives away free TikTok series funded by brand integrations and calls the brands “collaborators,” not sponsors.

Why it mattersThe same shift the creator-economy funding numbers have pointed to since issue 12, infrastructure and equity over one-off fees, now visible on the creator side of the table too. The creators big enough to say no are choosing fewer, deeper, equity-bearing relationships over volume.
Meta / Advertising Week New York · October 8, 2026

Meta makes AI video from a product photo a standard tool, not a stunt

Meta’s Advantage+ Creative can now generate a video ad directly from an advertiser’s existing static product photos, and the feature has moved from limited pilot to generally available for any advertiser. Meta’s own stated reason: more than 60% of time spent on Facebook and Instagram goes to video, while most advertisers’ asset libraries are still photos.

Why it mattersLast issue’s Goodwipes spot took an AI-native agency four people and four days to make. This is the same capability, free, inside the platform, for anyone running ads. The agency stunt and the platform default are converging faster than the production-speed story usually gets credit for.

Social trends

Ramalama Costume Walk (TikTok)

  • Low-angle clip that reveals a full Halloween costume step by step while walking to Roisin Murphy’s track “Ramalama (Bang Bang),” camera starting on dragging feet before pulling back to the full look.
Why it mattersA reveal format built around withholding information for exactly as long as a song’s intro lasts, not around the costume itself.

Pumpkin Head Illusion (TikTok)

  • Someone holds a real pumpkin up to the camera lens to cover a person’s head while that person dances or moves behind it, a one-prop, no-editing illusion.
Why it mattersZero production value, zero software, the entire trick is physical distance from the camera. The cheapest idea in the feed still beats a well-produced one this time of year.

Stop the Wedding, But (TikTok)

  • Photo-carousel confessional format opening on the caption “stop the wedding, but...” before a slide-by-slide story of a regret, doubt or secret tied to someone else’s wedding.
Why it mattersThe hook borrows its tension from reality-TV wedding shows without needing any footage from one, text and photos doing what video used to.

The historical bridge

New York, 1833

The newspaper that gave itself away to sell your attention instead

On September 3, 1833, a 23-year-old printer named Benjamin Day launched The Sun in New York at one cent a copy, a sixth of what established papers charged, hawked on the street by boys instead of delivered to paying subscribers. Within six months its circulation hit 8,000, twice its nearest competitor’s, built on short, plain-language crime and police reports instead of the political essays other papers ran for their party patrons. The price cut only worked because Day had already flipped who was paying: advertisers and street sales replaced the political-party funding that had bankrolled papers until then. The motto across the masthead, “It Shines for All,” was a circulation strategy wearing a mission statement.

Why it still holds. OpenAI’s new ad format (above) draws the same line Day drew in 1833: pay nothing or little and your attention is the product, pay a subscription and it isn’t. The platform picks which tier gets the ads, same as Day picked the penny price that forced his paper to live on advertising instead of political money. The mechanism is 193 years old, only the paper changed.
